name: Chronic kidney disease

matching.reasoningTemplate: Longstanding reduced renal function with anaemia and small kidneys indicates CKD rather than acute injury.

redFlags: Distinguish from AKI; manage complications (K⁺, acidosis, anaemia)

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e Ch.322 (Chronic Kidney Disease), pp.2385-2396; Ch.319 staging/clinical, pp.2361-2362 and Table 319-3 p.2362
clinicalPearls: Progression risk in CKD tracks three things together: the current GFR, the trajectory of GFR over time, and the degree of albuminuria - not GFR alone (p.2385).

Once nephron mass is reduced, surviving nephrons undergo compensatory hyperfiltration and hypertrophy; these short-term adaptations become maladaptive, driving glomerulosclerosis and ongoing GFR loss even after the original insult has resolved (p.2385-2386, 2396).
A normal serum creatinine can mask substantial GFR loss in older patients and women (lower muscle mass); an elderly woman with a 'normal' creatinine may have a GFR under 50 mL/min/1.73 m2 (p.2387).

Loss of urinary concentrating ability gives an obligate output of ~2 L/day and nocturia; paradoxically, resolution of nocturia may feel like improvement but can actually signal worsening oliguria (p.2362).

Cardiac troponin is frequently chronically elevated in CKD without acute ischemia - serial trending over hours is more informative than a single value, and persistently elevated levels independently predict adverse cardiovascular events (p.2392).
Most CKD patients die of cardiovascular disease before ever reaching stage 5; cardiovascular risk is increased roughly 10- to 200-fold versus age/sex-matched controls depending on stage (p.2391).

In advanced CKD a malnutrition-inflammation state can paradoxically reverse classic risk factors (lowering blood pressure and lipids) and is itself a marker of poor prognosis - so 'improving' numbers can be ominous (p.2392).

A drop in GFR of up to ~30% after starting an ACEi/ARB is often a benign reflection of relieved intraglomerular hyperfiltration; if stable it can be tolerated, but a progressive rise in creatinine suggests underlying renovascular disease (p.2392, 2396).

A normal-sized kidney does not exclude CKD: diabetic nephropathy (early), amyloidosis, and HIV nephropathy can show normal or enlarged kidneys despite advanced disease; polycystic kidneys are typically enlarged (p.2394-2395).
Hyperkalemia disproportionate to the GFR decline points to hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism (e.g., diabetes) or distal-nephron disease such as obstructive uropathy or sickle cell nephropathy (p.2389).
PTH is itself a uremic toxin - high levels are associated with muscle weakness, cardiac fibrosis, ESA-resistant anemia (via marrow fibrosis), and constitutional symptoms (p.2390).
Erythrocytosis rather than anemia can occur in some CKD-associated conditions: urinary tract obstruction, polycystic kidney disease, renovascular disease, and renal cell carcinoma (p.2362).
harrison.pathophysiology: CKD results from two overlapping processes: (1) initiating mechanisms specific to the underlying cause (developmental/genetic, immune-complex, inflammatory, metabolic, microvascular, or toxic injury to vascular, glomerular, or tubulointerstitial compartments), and (2) a nonspecific final common pathway in which loss of nephron mass triggers compensatory hyperfiltration and hypertrophy of remaining nephrons. Intrarenal renin-angiotensin activation with blunted tubuloglomerular feedback raises intraglomerular pressure; this adaptation becomes maladaptive, distorting glomerular architecture, impairing podocyte function and the filtration barrier, and producing progressive sclerosis and nephron dropout. The uremic syndrome arises from three spheres of dysfunction: accumulation of retained solutes (urea and creatinine are only readily-measured but incomplete surrogates for many retained toxins), loss of non-excretory kidney functions (fluid/electrolyte homeostasis, hormone production/regulation - EPO, calcitriol, with altered PTH, FGF-23, insulin), and progressive systemic inflammation (elevated CRP, falling albumin/fetuin) feeding a malnutrition-inflammation-atherosclerosis/calcification syndrome (p.2385-2389).
additionalDifferentials: Diabetic nephropathy (commonest cause in North America/Europe, usually type 2 DM) (p.2389)
Hypertension-associated CKD / nephrosclerosis, including ischemic and vascular kidney disease (p.2389)
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) and other cystic/tubulointerstitial nephropathy (p.2389)
APOL1-mediated kidney disease and FSGS (higher frequency in sub-Saharan African ancestry) (p.2386-2387)
Hereditary/genetic CKD - Alport syndrome (type IV collagen, hematuria + sensorineural hearing loss + lens defects), Fabry disease, cystinosis (p.2394)
Multiple myeloma (check serum/urine protein electrophoresis in patients >35 with unexplained CKD, especially with anemia and inappropriately normal/high calcium) (p.2394)
Reflux nephropathy (recurrent childhood UTI, asymmetric scarred kidneys) (p.2395)
nonInfectiousMimics: Acute or subacute kidney injury that is potentially reversible - the single most important distinction from true CKD; prior creatinine values establish chronicity (p.2395)

Acute-on-chronic kidney failure from a superimposed reversible insult: ECFV depletion (GI losses, over-diuresis), urinary tract infection, new obstructive uropathy, nephrotoxin/contrast/NSAID exposure, or flare of the primary disease (e.g., lupus, vasculitis) (p.2389, 2395-2396)
additionalInvestigations: Estimated GFR using race-free CKD-EPI or MDRD equations - valid only in steady state (creatinine not rising or falling); cystatin-C as an alternative marker where creatinine production is confounded by muscle mass/limb loss (p.2387, 2362)

Urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) on spot first-morning samples (replaces 24-h collection) - persistent elevation flags glomerular and systemic microvascular injury even with a negative dipstick (p.2387)
Kidney Failure Risk equation (age, sex, region, GFR, UACR) to predict progression to stage 5 (p.2387)
Serum/urine protein electrophoresis for myeloma in unexplained CKD >35y (p.2394)
Serologic workup if hematuria/proteinuria: ANA/lupus serology, hepatitis B and C, HIV (p.2394-2395)
Calcium, phosphate, PTH (and FGF-23 conceptually) for CKD-mineral bone disorder; hemoglobin, iron studies/transferrin saturation, ferritin, B12, folate for anemia (p.2394)

Renal ultrasound to assess kidney number, symmetry, size, masses and obstruction; bilaterally small kidneys indicate long-standing CKD; >1 cm length discrepancy suggests unilateral/renovascular disease (p.2394-2395)

Kidney biopsy reserved for early CKD with diagnostic uncertainty or suspected superimposed active process - NOT advised once kidneys are small/scarred (technically hazardous, scarring obscures diagnosis, no therapeutic window) (p.2395)

Genetic testing (large CKD gene panels, microarray, exome/genome sequencing) for familial disease, consanguinity, extrarenal/syndromic features, steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome, cystic disease, or young-onset unexplained CKD (p.2395)
redFlags: Uremic pericarditis (pleuritic chest pain with friction rub; ECG with PR depression and diffuse ST elevation) - absolute indication for urgent dialysis; risk of hemorrhagic effusion and tamponade, so dialyze without heparin (p.2392)
Asterixis, myoclonus, seizures, or coma in advanced untreated kidney failure - uremic encephalopathy (p.2393)
Peripheral neuropathy without another cause is an indication to start renal replacement therapy (p.2393)

Calciphylaxis - painful livedo reticularis and subcutaneous nodules progressing to ischemic skin necrosis/ulceration (legs, thighs, abdomen, breasts); warfarin is a risk factor and should be stopped (p.2390-2391)
Diuretic-resistant intractable edema and hypertension, refractory hyperkalemia, or refractory pulmonary edema in advanced CKD - indications to initiate dialysis (p.2389, 2392)
Accelerating rate of GFR decline - prompts search for a reversible superimposed acute/subacute process (p.2396)
Acute systemic features (fever, polyarthritis, rash) with renal impairment suggest an acute systemic illness rather than chronic CKD (p.2395)
harrison.prognosis: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality at every stage, and most patients die of it before reaching stage 5; only 30-45% of those who reach stage 5 have advanced cardiovascular complications at that point. Left ventricular hypertrophy and dilated cardiomyopathy are among the strongest predictors of cardiovascular death. Hyperphosphatemia, high FGF-23, and persistently elevated troponin independently predict worse cardiovascular outcomes. A superimposed malnutrition-inflammation-calcification state in advanced disease carries a poor prognosis. Nephrotic-range proteinuria and heavy persistent proteinuria predict faster progression and worse outcomes. Survivors of dialysis-requiring AKI are at high risk of progressive CKD, with up to ~10% developing ESKD (p.2384, 2391-2392, 2362).
pitfalls: Treating an elevated creatinine as chronic without checking prior values - missing a reversible acute or acute-on-chronic process (p.2395).
Assuming normal kidney size excludes CKD (diabetic nephropathy early, amyloid, HIV nephropathy retain normal/large kidneys) (p.2394-2395).

Stopping ACEi/ARB for a modest (<30%) non-progressive GFR fall - discontinuation in CKD is associated with increased death/cardiovascular events; the small drop usually reflects relieved hyperfiltration (p.2392).
Combining an ACE inhibitor with an ARB - greater incidence of AKI and adverse cardiac events; avoid dual blockade (p.2396).
Overlooking occult potassium sources (dietary salt substitutes) and potassium-retaining drugs (RAS inhibitors, MRAs, potassium-sparing diuretics) as causes of hyperkalemia (p.2389).
Gadolinium MRI contrast in advanced CKD - risk of nephrogenic systemic/fibrosing dermopathy; minimize in stage 3 and avoid in stages 4-5 unless essential (older agents) (p.2394).
Iodinated radiographic contrast - contrast-induced nephropathy, especially in diabetic nephropathy; avoid where possible (p.2395).
Pruritus and skin pigmentation often persist despite dialysis; first rule out unrelated causes (e.g., scabies) and treat hyperphosphatemia (p.2394).
Metformin and sulfonylureas are contraindicated below ~half-normal GFR; insulin requirements fall as renal degradation of insulin declines (p.2394).
harrison.severityClassification: KDIGO classification stratifies CKD by GFR category and albuminuria, both predicting all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, and progression. GFR categories: G1 >=90, G2 60-89, G3a 45-59, G3b 30-44, G4 15-29, G5 <15 mL/min/1.73 m2. Albuminuria (UACR) categories: A1 <30, A2 30-299, A3 >=300 mg/g. Harrison Table 319-3 stages (abnormality >3 months): Stage 1 (>60 with abnormal urinalysis/imaging), Stage 2 (>60, mild progression risk), Stage 3a (45-60), Stage 3b (30-45), Stage 4 (15-30, prepare for RRT), Stage 5 (<15, highest RRT need). Stages 1-2 are usually asymptomatic; complications emerge in stages 3-4; the full uremic syndrome appears at stage 5 (GFR <15) (p.2385-2388, 2362, Table 319-3).
